title: Should national service come back?

turns.speaker: Raj
turns.text: It's in the manifesto again. A year at eighteen, military or civic, and you choose which.

turns.speaker: Tor
turns.text: The military half is the bit the army itself doesn't want. Conscripts cost more to train and leave the moment they can.

turns.speaker: Elsie
turns.text: That's usually the killer argument and it's made by the people you'd expect to support it.

turns.speaker: Raj
turns.text: The civic version is more interesting, though. A year in care homes, conservation, that sort of thing.

turns.speaker: Tor
turns.text: Which is a real need. The worry is it becomes cheap labour propping up services that should be properly staffed.

turns.speaker: Tor
turns.text: You don't fix a care sector by handing it eighteen-year-olds for a year at a time.

turns.speaker: Elsie
turns.text: The social mixing argument is the one I find genuinely attractive. Most people now go through life meeting nobody from outside their own bracket.

turns.speaker: Raj
turns.text: Although that only works if it's universal. The moment there's an exemption, it's the same people again.

turns.speaker: Tor
turns.text: The countries that kept it tend to have small, broadly equal populations, which is doing a lot of the work people attribute to the policy.

turns.speaker: Raj
turns.text: So the thing being copied might be the society rather than the scheme.

turns.speaker: Elsie
turns.text: You could get most of the benefit voluntarily and paid, mind you. That exists and it's chronically underfunded.

turns.speaker: Tor
turns.text: Which is less satisfying than compelling people, politically speaking.

points: A proposal would require a year of military or civic service at eighteen.
Tor notes the armed forces themselves resist conscription, as conscripts cost more to train and leave quickly.
The civic option meets real needs but risks becoming cheap labour substituting for proper staffing.
Elsie finds the social mixing argument attractive, since people rarely meet others outside their own bracket.
Raj argues this requires universality, and exemptions always emerge.

Tor suggests countries with successful schemes are small and equal societies, so the society rather than the policy may explain the outcome; Elsie notes voluntary paid schemes already exist but are underfunded.
